hints: Look closely at what the $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ ion actually does to the hydrogen in the curly arrow diagram.
Notice the lone pair on oxygen forms a new O-H bond to make $(CH_3)_3COH$, so it is gaining a proton.
Recall the definition of a Bronsted-Lowry base and check how the C-I bond electrons move to decide if fission is homo or hetero.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction type**

Look at the starting haloalkane and the product. We lose H and I and gain a C=C double bond.

This is an elimination reaction, specifically E2, not substitution or hydrolysis.

**Follow what happens to the base**

The curly arrow starts from the lone pair on $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ and points to H.

$$ (CH_3)_3CO^- + H^+ \rightarrow (CH_3)_3COH $$
That means the ion accepts a proton to form an alcohol.

**Check the C-I bond fission**

The arrow from the C-H bond forms the C=C, and the arrow from the C-I bond goes fully onto I to give $:I^-$.

Both bonding electrons go to one atom, so this is heterolytic fission, with no change in oxidation number.

options.A: Correct. A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. Here $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ uses its lone pair to remove $H^+$ and forms $(CH_3)_3COH$, exactly as shown by the arrows.
options.B: Incorrect. An oxidising agent gains electrons and causes oxidation numbers to increase. Here oxidation numbers do not change, the tert-butoxide simply accepts a proton.
options.C: Incorrect. Homolytic fission gives one electron to each atom and forms radicals. Here the full arrow shows both electrons going to iodine to form $I^-$, so it is heterolytic fission.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrolysis uses water or aqueous $OH^-$ to replace a halogen with OH and form an alcohol. This reaction removes HI to form an alkene, so it is elimination (dehydrohalogenation).
